title: {{NAME}} and the Dinosaur Who Guarded the City
moral: Real strength is not about standing above others but about standing beside them when it counts.

pages.content:
The city of Halcyon was the kind of place that expected unusual things and had built the infrastructure to accommodate them. Its tallest building had a landing platform on the roof for exactly this reason. Its emergency systems had a protocol numbered 7-ALPHA-DEEP that no one had ever used and everyone hoped never to need.

On the night that protocol 7-ALPHA-DEEP was triggered, {{NAME}} was already in the air, his cerulean cape pulling against the updrafts between the towers, scanning the harbour where the signal had originated.

What he found was not what he expected. The anomaly in the harbour was not a threat. It was a titanosaur, a colossal long-neck the length of a city block, rising slowly from the deep water of the harbour channel with the bewildered carefulness of something that has arrived somewhere by accident and is trying very hard not to break anything. She had already overturned two empty barges, which she was clearly distressed about. She was trying, with limited success, to right them with a foreleg the size of a shipping container.

{{NAME}} hovered in the air before her enormous face and revised every plan he had arrived with.

pages.content:
The titanosaur's eyes were warm amber and the size of house windows. When {{NAME}} came close enough for her to focus on him properly, she went very still, with the touching caution of something large trying not to cause further unintended damage.

{{NAME}} floated at eye level and stayed there. He did not signal the city's response teams who were beginning to gather on the harbour walls. He did not activate his communicator. He just stayed at eye level with a titanosaur in a harbour in the middle of the night and let her decide whether he was something to fear.

She decided, after approximately forty seconds of amber-eyed assessment, that he was not. She exhaled through enormous nostrils and her breath hit him like a warm, fishy gust. He managed, just barely, not to be blown sideways.

The titanosaur made a sound then: low, questioning, somehow both enormous and plaintive. {{NAME}}'s face in the harbour light went from focused readiness to something entirely more open, something moved and gentle.

'I know,' he said, though he did not speak titanosaur. 'Let's figure it out together.'

pages.content:
Righting the barges was actually the easier part, once {{NAME}} and the titanosaur were working together. She was immensely strong and, once she understood what was being asked, immensely careful. {{NAME}} flew low to each barge in turn, attached the tow lines from the harbour bollards, and she drew them upright with a precision that would have impressed the harbour master greatly, if the harbour master had been in any state to be impressed rather than simply staring from the harbour wall.

The harder part was the deep-water channel. The titanosaur had come up it from below, from some passage between the prehistoric ocean and this one that had opened without warning, and it appeared to have partially collapsed behind her. She could not go back the way she had come.

{{NAME}} flew every inch of the harbour perimeter, thinking fast. His communicator crackled: the city's other responders were asking for instruction. He gave them one instruction only: open the North Gate to the tidal estuary and clear the channel markers.

Then he flew back to the titanosaur's eye and extended one hand, palm up, and simply pointed.

pages.content:
The titanosaur understood his pointing hand. She followed him through the harbour with extraordinary care, her body a slow moving island in the dark water, her wake lapping at the stone walls in long, gentle pulses. Every boat in the harbour shifted. The channel markers glowed in the dark like a trail of breadcrumbs.

When she reached the North Gate and the open estuary beyond, she paused. She turned her enormous neck and looked back at {{NAME}} in a way that was unmistakably a look of consideration, of measuring something significant and finding it sufficient.

Then she gave that low, warm, questioning sound again. But this time it was not a question. It was the answer to one.

{{NAME}} watched her move out through the North Gate into the dark estuary, her outline visible against the harbour lights long after the water had swallowed everything else, and then not visible at all. He hovered alone above the cleared harbour in the midnight air.

The city exhaled. The responders on the harbour wall were quiet. The water stilled, slow and glittering, as though the harbour itself was deciding what it thought of what had just happened.

pages.content:
{{NAME}} landed on the harbour wall after she was gone. The stone was cold under his boots and the harbour smelled of salt and displaced prehistoric water. The responders on the wall gave him room, because that seemed like the right thing to do.

He sat on a bollard and looked at the dark open estuary where she had disappeared and thought about the size of the ocean and the extraordinary things it contained.

A junior responder, very young, sidled up and sat on the next bollard without speaking. After a while she said, carefully: 'Is she going to be all right out there?'

{{NAME}} thought about this with the seriousness it deserved. 'She's been in a larger, older ocean than this one,' he said, 'for a very long time.' He paused. 'I think she knows a few things about all right.'

The junior responder nodded and seemed satisfied. The harbour water went still.

{{NAME}}'s cape pooled around him on the bollard, midnight-blue and silver in the harbour light. His eyes went slow and warm and finally, finally, closed.

Goodnight, guardian. Dream of deep water and great distances, and wonder whether she found what she was looking for.
